title: How RAG works, step by step
question: How does retrieval augmented generation (RAG) work?

problem.statement: Design an AI assistant that answers questions about your company’s own documents, with answers you can trust and trace back to a source.
example: “What is our refund window for annual plans?”
If the documents don’t say, it says so
constraints: 50,000 pages of internal documents, updated every week
problem.followUp: How would you know the assistant is getting it right?

steps.caption: What the interviewer is really asking.

plain.asking: Build an AI that *looks things up in your documents before it answers*, and shows where it found the answer.
points: *Must work:* answer from your own documents, and cite them.
*Must be honest:* if the documents don’t say, say so.
*Out of scope:* training a model from scratch.

steps.caption: Start with a plain AI model. You ask it: “What is our refund window?” It answers from whatever it learned during training.

items.label: AI MODEL (LLM)
items.note: A large language model: great at writing, but it only knows what it was trained on.

steps.caption: But your refund policy was never in its training data. It may say it doesn’t know, or *confidently invent* an answer. That is a hallucination.

items.label: AI MODEL (LLM)
items.note: A large language model: great at writing, but it only knows what it was trained on.

steps.caption: Idea: paste your documents into the question. The AI reads them first, then answers from them. Now it can use *your* policy.

steps.caption: So send only the few paragraphs that matter for *this* question. That needs a way to *find* them. The finding step is the “R” in RAG: Retrieval.

items.label: YOUR DOCUMENTS
items.note: Policies, manuals, tickets, wikis: whatever the AI should be able to answer from.

items.label: AI MODEL (LLM)
items.note: A large language model: great at writing, but it only knows what it was trained on.

steps.caption: First, cut every document into small pieces called *chunks*: a few paragraphs each, with a little overlap so no sentence is split in half.

items.label: YOUR DOCUMENTS
items.note: Policies, manuals, tickets, wikis: whatever the AI should be able to answer from.

items.label: CHUNKS
items.note: Small pieces of the documents: a few paragraphs each, with a little overlap.

steps.caption: An *embedding model* reads each chunk and outputs a list of numbers that captures its *meaning*. Similar meanings give similar numbers.

items.label: CHUNKS
items.note: Small pieces of the documents: a few paragraphs each, with a little overlap.

items.label: EMBEDDING MODEL
items.note: Turns text into a list of numbers that captures its meaning.

steps.caption: Picture those lists of numbers as points on a map. Refund chunks land together, shipping chunks elsewhere. *Close on the map means close in meaning.*

items.label: VECTOR DATABASE
items.note: Stores every chunk as a point, and finds the points nearest to a query, fast.

steps.caption: Every chunk’s point goes into a *vector database*, built to find the nearest points fast. All of this happens once, ahead of time, before anyone asks.

check.question: Why turn chunks into numbers (embeddings) instead of searching for the words themselves?
options: Numbers capture meaning, so “money back” can find “refund”
Numbers are cheaper to store than words
Words can’t be searched at all
check.explain: Embeddings capture *meaning*, so a question can find a chunk that uses different words. Exact words still matter sometimes; the next lesson fixes that.

steps.caption: Now someone asks: “How long do customers have to get their money back?” The *same* embedding model turns the question into a point on the map.

items.label: EMBEDDING MODEL
items.note: The SAME model that embedded the chunks. Different models give maps that can’t be compared.

items.label: VECTOR DATABASE
items.note: Stores every chunk as a point, and finds the points nearest to a query, fast.

steps.caption: The database returns the chunks nearest to the question: the top 3, called “top-k”. The question never said “refund”, yet meaning put it right beside them.

items.label: EMBEDDING MODEL
items.note: The SAME model that embedded the chunks. Different models give maps that can’t be compared.

items.label: VECTOR DATABASE
items.note: Stores every chunk as a point, and finds the points nearest to a query, fast.

steps.caption: Those chunks go into a prompt with the question and one rule: “answer only from this context, and say where it came from.”

items.label: EMBEDDING MODEL
items.note: The SAME model that embedded the chunks. Different models give maps that can’t be compared.

items.label: VECTOR DATABASE
items.note: Stores every chunk as a point, and finds the points nearest to a query, fast.

items.label: PROMPT
items.note: Question + the retrieved chunks + the rules for answering.

steps.caption: The AI reads the chunks and writes: “30 days from purchase (Refund Policy v3, §2).” It can *name its source*, because the source was in front of it.

steps.caption: That is *RAG*: Retrieval-Augmented Generation. *Retrieve* the right chunks, *augment* the prompt with them, then let the AI *generate* the answer.

check.question: A RAG answer is wrong. What do you check first?
options: Whether the right chunk was in the retrieved results
Whether the AI model is too small
check.explain: If the right chunk never reached the prompt, no model can answer correctly. Check *retrieval* first, then *generation*.

steps.caption: The big idea: don’t make the AI memorise your data. *Look up the relevant pieces at question time* and hand them over. Next: where this basic version breaks.
